content: Between 2012 and 2022, Association Xenon has facilitated care for 104 individuals living with HIV, 853 individuals with positive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) test results, 5,130 individuals with hepatitis C virus (HCV) antibodies, and 337 individuals diagnosed with syphilis. From 2018 to 2022, Xenon implemented point-of-care RNA HCV testing, identifying 1,494 clients positive for anti-HCV antibodies. Of these, 82% (1,225) underwent HCV RNA testing, 56% (691) were confirmed to have active HCV infection, and 68% (470) received free direct-acting antiviral treatment through the National Hepatitis Elimination Programme. These efforts were instrumental in persuading the government to invest in community-based testing for people who inject drugs and other key populations. The government now fully funds testing for HIV, HBsAg, HCV RNA, and syphilis. Globally, men living with HIV aged 15 years and older are less likely than women in the same age group to know their HIV status, initiate treatment, or achieve viral suppression. These disparities are most pronounced in sub-Saharan Africa. Men from key populations bear a significant burden of HIV, and outside Africa, they account for more new HIV infections than women in similar populations. WHO guidance emphasizes the need for a strategic mix of differentiated HIV testing services (HTS) to reach more men and link them to prevention and treatment services. This includes facility-based, community-based, network-based, and self-testing services. Reducing stigma and fear, increasing access points, and integrating HIV testing with other health services such as STI, TB, and viral hepatitis testing are critical strategies. Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) remains a priority in many countries, and HIV testing, including self-testing, should be fully integrated into service delivery. Adolescents and young people (ages 10–24) are particularly vulnerable to HIV and are less likely to access testing services compared to adults. Barriers include stigma, discrimination, and misaligned age-of-consent policies. WHO recommends revising these policies to empower adolescents to make health decisions independently. Lay providers, including trained young people, can safely and effectively conduct HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. Differentiated HTS approaches, such as facility-based, community-based, network-based, and self-testing, are essential to reach this population. For sexually active adolescents, particularly young women in high HIV burden settings, focused self-testing for HIV and syphilis, as well as community-based testing, is recommended. HPV vaccination should be offered to girls aged 9–14 as per national guidelines. For pregnant and postpartum women, WHO recommends testing for HIV, syphilis, and HBsAg at least once during pregnancy, ideally at the first antenatal care visit. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can be used as the first test in antenatal care settings. Pregnant women testing negative for HBsAg can be offered HBV vaccination. Services for pregnant and postpartum women should be integrated to include screening and treatment for other infections, HIV prevention, and sexual and reproductive health services. Pregnant women living with HIV should initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) immediately and continue for life. For infants and children, early diagnosis and treatment are critical, as untreated HIV-infected infants face high mortality rates within the first year of life. WHO recommends virological testing for all HIV-exposed infants at 4–6 weeks of age or as soon as possible thereafter. Point-of-care nucleic acid testing (NAT) should be used to diagnose HIV in infants under 18 months of age. Infants with an initial positive virological test result should start ART immediately while awaiting confirmatory testing. Testing should also be offered to children with unknown HIV status who present at inpatient wards, malnutrition clinics, or TB clinics in high HIV burden settings. Network-based testing, family and household testing, and social network testing are recommended for children of people living with HIV. For children and adolescents who have been sexually abused, WHO recommends HIV PEP, emergency contraception, and presumptive STI treatment where laboratory testing is not feasible. In Ghana, the introduction of dual HIV/syphilis testing in antenatal care (ANC) settings significantly increased syphilis testing coverage from 53% in 2018 to 91% in 2021. This initiative, supported by stakeholder engagement and training, reduced procurement costs and improved testing efficiency. Challenges included incomplete training of providers and suboptimal partner treatment. Nevertheless, the adoption of dual testing has been critical in advancing Ghana’s progress toward the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and HBV. For infants and children, WHO emphasizes the importance of early infant diagnosis (EID) and treatment initiation. NAT at birth or within two days is recommended, complemented by additional testing as per national algorithms. Same-day point-of-care testing significantly increases the likelihood of treatment initiation within 60 days compared to laboratory-based testing. Scaling up access to testing and treatment for infants and children is essential to eliminate pediatric HIV/AIDS by 2030. Comprehensive testing approaches, including facility-based, network-based, and community-based strategies, are necessary to reach this goal.
